body.text: The Narendra Modi government’s prickliness to criticism has been underscored yet again by its denial of entry to foreign delegates participating in the Bharat Summit organized by the Congress party-led Telangana government in Hyderabad on November 13-14.

“115 of the 315 speakers whom the External Affairs Ministry had cleared for the event ended up being refused entry to India or having their visas cancelled, apparently on the instructions of the Ministry of Home Affairs,” Congress party parliamentarian Shashi Tharoor said in a post on X.
The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) has justified the decision, stating that “visa matters are sovereign functions of any country or any government.” The MHA has remained silent on the matter.

While “granting visas is undoubtedly the government’s prerogative, rescinding and blocking visas after the MEA’s political clearance suggests deep paranoia,” Pushparaj Deshpande, founder of the Samruddha Bharat Foundation that curated the event, told The Diplomat.

The Bharat Summit saw around 1,000 people, including leaders of progressive parties, academics, activists, journalists, and policymakers from around 70 countries, deliberate on issues like authoritarianism, inequality, and the new global order. The Modi government was no doubt apprehensive that the progressive participants would criticize its policies and actions. So it chose to muffle these voices by denying them entry into India.
Among the foreign delegates whose visas were canceled was Norwegian journalist Helle Lyng, who was scheduled to speak at a panel on the future of the media.

Lyng came under the global spotlight during Modi’s visit to Norway in May this year. When Modi walked off the stage at a joint press briefing without taking a single question from journalists, Lyng had shouted: “Prime Minister Modi, why don’t you take some questions from the freest press in the world?” The embarrassment she caused with that question would have brought her into the government’s crosshairs.

Another delegate who was kept from attending the Bharat Summit was Alessio De Giorgi of the European Democratic Party (EDP). When De Giorgi applied for his visa, the Indian consul in Brussels reportedly summoned him. He was shown a video of the EDP expressing support for Congress leader Rahul Gandhi and was told by the consul that the EDP’s support for the Congress party was “foreign interference.” De Giorgi was denied a visa.
The Modi government’s action is not surprising. It has happened several times since it took over the reins in 2014.

In 2024, for instance, Nitasha Kaul, a British academic of Indian origin who was to speak at a conference organized by Karnataka’s Congress government, was deported from Bengaluru airport. Her Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI) status, which allows its holders a lifetime entry to India, was canceled subsequently, as she was “found to be indulging in anti-India activities, motivated by malice and complete disregard for facts or history,” a government notice to her said, adding that she “regularly target[s] India and its institutions on the matters of India’s sovereignty.”
A critic of the Modi government, Kaul had testified before the U.S. House Committee on Foreign Affairs in October 2019 on the human rights situation in Kashmir after the revocation of Article 370.

India has become a hostile place to research, speak, or write about. Journalists critical of the Modi government are intimidated by intelligence agencies, bullied and threatened by online trolls, subjected to death threats, jailed for exposing corruption of business corporations, and even charged and jailed under India’s draconian anti-terrorism laws.

Those threatening journalists are not random goons bullying media persons whose views they disagree with. They are in fact linked to the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party, and are even followed by Modi. “It is all well organized and has political sanction,” Ravish Kumar, a former NDTV journalist and now a YouTuber, told The Hindu in 2018. Rarely do the police take action against the “troll armies.”

It has not been easy for foreign correspondents either to work in India. They are denied permission to visit several Indian states. Their visas are not extended. In 2022, the MHA revoked the journalism permit of French journalist Vanessa Dougnac, who was the South Asia correspondent for several French publications for over two decades, alleging that her “malicious” work created a “biased negative perception” of India.
Not surprisingly, India’s ranking on the World Freedom Index has fallen over the past decade, from 136 out of 180 countries in 2015 to 157 in 2026.

The Modi government has also sought to pressure critics living abroad by revoking their OCI status. In November 2019, author Aatish Taseer, who was born in the U.K. and raised in India, was stripped of his OCI status. The MHA claimed that Taseer had “concealed the fact that his late father was of Pakistani origin” — his father was Salman Taseer, a governor of Pakistani Punjab, who was assassinated for his opposition to Pakistan’s blasphemy laws — and was therefore ineligible for OCI status,

However, the Home Ministry’s decision may have had more to do with Aatish Taseer’s writings. Amid general elections in April-May 2019, Taseer wrote an article titled “India’s Divider in Chief,” which was published in TIME magazine. The piece was highly critical of Modi’s rule.

The Modi government has weaponized OCI status to silence critical voices in the Indian diaspora. Ashok Swain, an Indian-origin Swedish academic, has seen his OCI status canceled twice. Swain’s writings, the government said, have “tarnished the image of the country and its institutions in the eyes of the international community.”

“The government’s action was connected to my public criticism of the Modi government’s policies,” Swain told The Diplomat. He took the cancellation of his OCI status to the courts twice. Each time, the Delhi High Court set aside the cancelation order. Yet his OCI status has not been reinstated. “I have not regained the ability to enter India. The government has continued to pursue action against me, including a separate entry ban, and has initiated proceedings to cancel my OCI status for a third time,” Swain said.
Swain’s posts on X have been withheld in India, preventing his views from being read in India.

Scores of scholars have been denied visas to attend conferences or do research work in India. Francesca Orsini, a U.K.-based Hindi scholar, was deported from India for “visa violations.” Indian origin anti-caste activist Kshama Sawant was repeatedly denied an emergency visa to visit India. In 2020, Sawant had introduced a resolution in the Seattle City Council against the Modi government’s enactment of discriminatory citizenship laws.

The Modi government has canceled the OCI status of scores of people. According to government data obtained under the Right to Information Act, it revoked 57 OCI Cards in 2024 alone, almost half of all cancellations in ten years.

If the government’s objective in weaponizing visas and OCI status is to burnish India’s image, this is clearly not working. News emerging from the Bharat Summit was mainly about the visa denials. It showcased the authoritarian slide in India.

As Deshpande observed, the Modi government is “tarnishing India’s global reputation by vilifying policymakers from friendly governments as regime-change conspirators. This severely undermines the national interest.”
